metadata.title: Improving Security and Performance of Financial RESTful APIs Using ChatGPT in ASP.NET Core
metadata.degree: Master of Science in Information Technology

slides.title: Final Thesis Defense
slides.keyMessage: This study evaluates AI-assisted remediation through measured software evidence, not trust in generated code.

visibleContent.subtitle: Improving Security and Performance of Financial RESTful APIs Using ChatGPT in ASP.NET Core
lines: Advisor: Assistant Professor Dr. Darun Kesrarat

slides.speakerNotes: Good morning, and thank you for the opportunity to present my final thesis. My research investigates whether ChatGPT, used through the Codex coding environment, can help improve a financial accounting RESTful API in three measurable areas: code quality, security, and performance. The important point is that the model is not treated as an autonomous developer. It acts as an advisor. Every accepted change is reviewed by a human, isolated on a Git branch, and verified with the same tool that identified the original problem. Today I will explain the method, the measured results, the limitations, and the later GPT-5.4 versus GPT-5.5 comparison.
slides.transition: I will begin with the structure of the defense and the practical problem behind the study.
slides.overclaimWarning: Do not say that ChatGPT independently fixed the system.

slides.title: Defense Roadmap
slides.keyMessage: The defense moves from problem to method, evidence, comparison, and defensible conclusion.
slides.speakerNotes: The presentation follows five stages. First, I will define the practical problem and research gap. Second, I will explain the branch-isolated research design and the evaluation tools. Third, I will present the measured SonarQube, OWASP ZAP, and JMeter results. Fourth, I will discuss the GPT-5.4 versus GPT-5.5 comparison and the controlled new-API retest. Finally, I will state the contributions, limitations, and conclusion. Detailed branch, endpoint, and metric evidence is available in the appendix if the committee would like to inspect it during questions.
slides.transition: The starting point is a practical software-engineering problem in financial APIs.
slides.overclaimWarning: Keep this slide under one minute.

slides.title: One API, Three Failure Modes
slides.keyMessage: Security, performance, and maintainability failures require different evidence and must be improved without breaking accounting behavior.

pillars.label: Maintainability
pillars.detail: Code smells, complexity, duplication, quality gate

slides.speakerNotes: A financial API can fail in three different ways. First, a security weakness can expose identities, balances, or audit records. Second, a performance bottleneck can make reporting or posting unusable under load. Third, maintainability problems make future defects more likely and slow down remediation. These failures are detected by different tools and normally handled in separate workflows. The research asks whether an LLM can help interpret all three classes of evidence while preserving essential accounting rules, authorization boundaries, audit semantics, and regression tests. This is a harder and more realistic question than asking whether an AI can generate code that compiles.
slides.transition: Existing research covers code generation extensively, but this tool-guided remediation workflow is less studied.
slides.overclaimWarning: Do not imply that static-analysis findings are equivalent to exploitable vulnerabilities.

slides.title: Research Gap
slides.keyMessage: Most LLM-for-software-engineering work emphasizes generation; this study evaluates scanner-guided remediation across three independent gates.
slides.speakerNotes: The literature shows strong interest in code generation, code completion, and developer productivity. It also warns that generated code can introduce weaknesses when accepted without review. A smaller area of research is using an LLM as an advisor that receives structured findings from static analysis, security scanning, and load testing, then proposes fixes that are independently remeasured. This thesis addresses that gap with one financial ASP.NET Core API and a combined three-tool workflow. The contribution is therefore not a new AI model. It is an evidence-controlled way to evaluate AI-assisted remediation in a realistic codebase.
slides.transition: From that gap, the study defines three direct research questions.
slides.overclaimWarning: Describe the contribution as a workflow and empirical case study, not a universal theory.

slides.title: Research Questions
slides.keyMessage: The study tests measurable change in code quality, security, and performance under a controlled acceptance workflow.

questions: RQ1: Can tool-guided ChatGPT recommendations reduce measured code-quality findings without regression?
RQ2: Can they clear gated security alerts while preserving role-based access?
RQ3: Can they reduce tail latency and maintain zero-error behavior under load?

slides.speakerNotes: The research questions align directly with the three evaluation tools. RQ1 asks whether SonarQube findings can be reduced while quality gate, coverage, and duplication do not regress. RQ2 asks whether ZAP High, Medium, and Low alerts on business endpoints can be cleared while authentication and role-based authorization continue to work. RQ3 asks whether JMeter p95 and p99 latency improve across normal, soak, and spike profiles while error rate remains acceptable. This direct mapping is important because the conclusions are based on observable measures, not the model's own explanation of its changes.
slides.transition: To answer these questions, I used a production-complexity accounting API as the unit of analysis.
slides.overclaimWarning: Do not introduce developer-productivity claims; no human-subject productivity study was performed.

slides.title: System Under Study
slides.keyMessage: The unit of analysis covers complete accounting workflows rather than a toy endpoint.

visibleContent.stack: ASP.NET Core 8 | SQL Server | JWT/RBAC | React/Vite evidence client

slides.speakerNotes: The system under study is an ASP.NET Core 8 financial accounting API backed by SQL Server. Its endpoint groups include authentication, users, chart of accounts, journal entries, accounting periods, trial balance, profit and loss, balance sheet, account ledger, and audit logs. This scope matters because the system includes read and write operations, bulk posting, protected administrative actions, financial calculations, and auditability. A React and Vite client was later added as a live validation artifact, but the measured security and performance conclusions come from the API tools, not from the user interface.
slides.transition: The central control is that each class of remediation is isolated from the same baseline.
slides.overclaimWarning: Call it production-complexity, not a deployed production banking system.

slides.title: Branch-Isolated Research Design
slides.keyMessage: Every tool-specific result is compared against the same baseline on an isolated branch.

visibleContent.control: Same API, database, host, and measurement tool

slides.speakerNotes: The baseline branch is baseline-v0.1. Static-analysis fixes are applied only on baseline-sonarqube-v1, security fixes only on baseline-zap-v1, and performance fixes only on baseline-jmeter-v1. Each branch is remeasured with the same tool that produced its baseline evidence. The runtime, SQL Server database, host, and seeded data are kept consistent. This design improves attribution because a SonarQube change cannot be credited for a JMeter result from a different branch. It does not create a randomized experiment, but it is a stronger control than applying every suggestion to one changing branch.
slides.transition: The work on each branch follows the same four-phase evidence cycle.
slides.overclaimWarning: Use 'supports attribution' rather than 'proves causation.'

slides.title: Four-Phase Evidence Workflow
slides.keyMessage: The workflow accepts a fix only after the original measurement is repeated.
slides.speakerNotes: The workflow has four phases. First, capture the baseline and preserve the raw tool finding. Second, provide the finding and relevant source context to ChatGPT or Codex and obtain a candidate fix. Third, a human reviews the recommendation, applies only the acceptable change, and runs focused regression tests. Fourth, the same measurement tool is rerun and the before-and-after evidence is compared. Failed or inapplicable recommendations are not counted as improvements. This scanner-gated loop is the operational contribution of the study and is reusable in a CI/CD review process.
slides.transition: The environment and seeded data were held constant so those comparisons were repeatable.
slides.overclaimWarning: The diagram describes acceptance control, not full automation.

slides.title: Environment and Seeded Dataset
slides.keyMessage: All comparisons used one fixed local environment and a repeatable accounting dataset.

facts: Same host for baseline and fixes

slides.speakerNotes: All main comparisons used the same Windows 11 host, ASP.NET Core 8 runtime, local SQL Server Financial database, and seeded data process. The dataset contains 120 accounts, 30,000 journal entries, and at least 5,000 posted entries for report-generation paths. The authenticated roles are Admin, FinanceManager, User, and Auditor. JMeter runs in a fixed version 5.5 container, and ZAP uses the stable container image. This environment is repeatable, but it is still one local machine, so absolute latency values should not be generalized to cloud deployment performance.
slides.transition: Within that environment, five independent gates decide whether a change is acceptable.
slides.overclaimWarning: Do not describe the seeded data as a public financial dataset or real customer data.

slides.title: Evaluation Gates
slides.keyMessage: No single metric is allowed to stand in for overall software quality.
slides.speakerNotes: Five gates are combined. SonarQube measures retained findings, code smells, coverage, duplication, and quality-gate status. OWASP ZAP measures baseline and authenticated alert severity and affected endpoints. JMeter measures average, p95, p99, throughput, error rate, soak behavior, and spike recovery. Dotnet tests check functional regressions, and Git branch and commit evidence preserves traceability. The study does not treat a clean SonarQube result as proof of security, or faster latency as proof of correctness. The tools answer different questions and must be interpreted together.
slides.transition: The model sits inside this gate structure as an advisor, not as the final decision-maker.
slides.overclaimWarning: Never merge SonarQube, ZAP, and JMeter into one unsupported composite score.

slides.title: Human-in-the-Loop Use of ChatGPT/Codex
slides.keyMessage: Human review, accounting invariants, and remeasurement bound the model's role.

visibleContent.boundary: Acceptance is determined by evidence, not model confidence

slides.speakerNotes: The model receives the raw finding, relevant source files, and explicit constraints. It proposes a candidate patch. The human developer checks authorization, validation, idempotency, concurrency, audit writes, accounting periods, balancing, reconciliation, database consistency, and public contracts before accepting the change. Focused tests are run, followed by the original measurement tool. This design reduces the risk of plausible but incorrect AI recommendations. It also means the thesis evaluates an AI-assisted engineering process, not the model in isolation from human judgment.
slides.transition: With the method established, I will now present the three measured result streams.
slides.overclaimWarning: Avoid saying the model understood accounting rules; the workflow enforced them.

slides.title: SonarQube: Clean Closure Without Coverage Loss
slides.keyMessage: Retained findings fell from 28 to 0 while measured coverage and duplication remained stable.
slides.speakerNotes: SonarQube provides the cleanest closure result. Retained C# findings decreased from 28 to zero. Code smells decreased from 21 to zero, while bugs, vulnerabilities, and security hotspots stayed at zero. The final quality gate was OK. Coverage remained 74.3 percent and duplicated-line density remained zero, so the improvement was not achieved by removing tests or duplicating code. Representative changes included replacing a long controller signature with a request DTO, using asynchronous application startup, replacing repeated literals with named constants, and cleaning infrastructure templates.
slides.transition: Static quality closed cleanly; the security result requires a separate interpretation of gated and informational alerts.
slides.overclaimWarning: Do not call the 28 retained findings 28 vulnerabilities; 21 were code smells.

slides.title: OWASP ZAP: Business-Endpoint Gates Cleared
slides.keyMessage: All gated High, Medium, and Low business-endpoint alerts were cleared; informational observations remained reportable.
slides.speakerNotes: ZAP was run in passive baseline mode and authenticated API mode. In the baseline scan, Medium alerts decreased from two to zero and Low alerts from six to zero. In the authenticated scan, Low alerts decreased from three to zero. High alerts were zero before and after. Informational observations remained and are reported rather than hidden. The main fixes involved applying security headers before Swagger and OpenAPI middleware, reducing exposed diagnostic UI surface, and updating vulnerable dependencies. The defensible claim is that the pre-registered High, Medium, and Low gate was met on business endpoints, not that every possible security weakness was eliminated.
slides.transition: Performance was evaluated separately across normal, sustained, and burst workloads.
slides.overclaimWarning: Say 'gated business-endpoint alerts,' not 'the API is completely secure.'

slides.title: JMeter: Five Workload Profiles
slides.keyMessage: Normal and stress profiles measure different aspects of system behavior and must not be collapsed into one latency number.
slides.speakerNotes: JMeter uses five profiles. The p50, p100, and p500 profiles evaluate normal through heavy concurrency. The soak profile checks sustained behavior over time, and the spike profile tests response under a sudden burst and the ability to recover. For each profile, the study records p95 and p99 latency, throughput, and error rate. Soak and spike also include drift measures. Tail latency is emphasized because averages can hide slow requests. A lower p95 means that 95 percent of requests complete below that threshold.
slides.transition: Across these profiles, latency improved substantially, but the stress interpretation remains conservative.
slides.overclaimWarning: Explain p95 correctly; it is not the average response time.

slides.title: JMeter: Large p95 Reductions, One Honest Caveat
slides.keyMessage: All five total p95 values improved with zero core-profile errors, while mixed-workload drift remains a limitation.

visibleContent.callout: 0.00% error rate on p50, p100, and p500
visibleContent.caveat: Mixed-workload soak/spike drift heuristics still fail

slides.speakerNotes: The total p95 latency improved in every profile. At p50 it decreased from 49.45 to 13 milliseconds. At p100 it decreased from 261.95 to 34 milliseconds. At p500 it decreased from 176 to 28 milliseconds. Soak decreased from 970.95 to 56 milliseconds, and spike from 6,795 to 1,420 milliseconds. Error rate remained zero for the three core profiles. The main optimizations involved removing report-snapshot writes from read paths, reusing aggregated balances, adding indexes, caching ledger output, and reducing repeated query work. However, the report keeps an honest caveat: the mixed-workload drift heuristic still fails because the final window is compositionally heavier. Endpoint latency improved, but the original drift rule does not fully separate workload composition from degradation.
slides.transition: Performance improvements are acceptable only if accounting and authorization behavior remains intact.
slides.overclaimWarning: Do not claim that every endpoint or every stability heuristic passed.

slides.title: Integrity Was a Non-Negotiable Constraint
slides.keyMessage: Faster or cleaner code was rejected if it weakened authorization, balancing, period, audit, or reconciliation rules.
slides.speakerNotes: This is a financial API, so quality cannot be reduced to scanner counts and latency. The review process preserves JWT authentication and role-based authorization for Admin, FinanceManager, User, and Auditor. It also protects journal balancing, accounting-period constraints, idempotency, concurrency checks, audit writes, database consistency, and reconciliation integrity. The application evidence shows role-aware navigation and read-only behavior for the Auditor role. These controls are not proof of formal financial certification, but they demonstrate that the remediation workflow did not intentionally trade correctness and access control for faster measurements.
slides.transition: The web application makes several of those API and authorization behaviors visible to a reviewer.
slides.overclaimWarning: Do not claim formal accounting certification or exhaustive security verification.
evidenceRefs: API endpoint and role coverage, pp. 30-32

slides.title: Working Application Evidence
slides.keyMessage: The screenshots demonstrate the user-visible path through authentication, reporting, audit, and role restrictions.

screens.caption: Admin dashboard and live API counts

slides.speakerNotes: The React and Vite client is a validation artifact for the API. It demonstrates login, role-aware navigation, account balances, financial reports, audit logs, and expandable journal-entry debit and credit lines. The Auditor screenshot is particularly useful because it shows restricted navigation and read-only account access. These screenshots support the claim that the API behavior is accessible through a real client. They do not replace the tool measurements or regression tests; they complement them with user-visible evidence.
slides.transition: The completed report also includes a controlled comparison between GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.5.
slides.overclaimWarning: Do not present screenshots as security-test evidence by themselves.

slides.title: GPT-5.4 vs GPT-5.5: Trade-offs, Not a Universal Winner
slides.keyMessage: SonarQube is a tie, residual ZAP cleanliness favors GPT-5.4, and balanced JMeter behavior with smaller patches favors GPT-5.5.
slides.speakerNotes: The normalized model comparison does not support a universal winner. Both models reduced SonarQube code smells from 21 to zero and reached the same 74.3 percent coverage. GPT-5.4 produced cleaner residual ZAP output. GPT-5.5 passed the business-endpoint gate but retained more Swagger, static-asset, and local-transport observations. In JMeter, GPT-5.4 was slightly faster on selected p100, p500, and soak tail metrics, but it introduced a severe p50 tail-latency regression. GPT-5.5 produced the more balanced profile and the strongest spike p99 and throughput outcome. GPT-5.5 also used fewer source and test files in the ZAP and JMeter patches. The conclusion depends on which quality dimension is weighted most heavily.
slides.transition: A later controlled retest corrected an important opportunity imbalance in the new-API comparison.
slides.overclaimWarning: Never say GPT-5.5 won every tool or is universally better.

slides.title: New-API v2 Controlled Retest
slides.keyMessage: After equalizing the correction opportunity, the measured SonarQube and ZAP outcomes are ties; JMeter remains incomplete.
slides.speakerNotes: The new-API v2 retest gave both Sonar candidates the same scan, correction, and rescan opportunity. Both reached zero measured Sonar issues, zero bugs, zero code smells, and an OK gate. GPT-5.4 had a 1.4 percentage-point coverage advantage. Both ZAP candidates reduced normalized business-alert instances from 36 to 12 with identical severity and endpoint coverage. Their full public test suites passed. However, there is no valid GPT-5.4 JMeter remediation candidate; its worktree matches the challenge baseline. Therefore, no overall three-tool winner is recorded. This is not missing decoration; it is a validity boundary that prevents an unfair comparison.
slides.transition: These results lead to three concrete contributions.
slides.overclaimWarning: Do not score the unavailable JMeter track or treat the baseline as GPT-5.4 output.

slides.title: Contributions
slides.keyMessage: The thesis contributes measured evidence, a reusable control workflow, and transparent limits on AI-assisted remediation.

contributions.label: Empirical
contributions.detail: Measured before/after evidence on one production-complexity API

contributions.label: Practical
contributions.detail: Traceable prompts, patches, tests, screenshots, and tool outputs

slides.speakerNotes: The thesis makes three contributions. Empirically, it provides measured before-and-after evidence across static quality, security scanning, and load testing on one production-complexity accounting API. Methodologically, it defines a reusable branch-isolated, scanner-gated workflow for accepting or rejecting LLM recommendations. Practically, it preserves traceability from finding to prompt, candidate patch, human decision, focused test, and rerun. The later model comparison adds evidence that smaller patches and balanced behavior can matter as much as winning an individual metric. The thesis does not claim a new algorithm or universal model ranking.
slides.transition: The value of those contributions depends on keeping their limitations visible.
slides.overclaimWarning: Do not describe a single-system case study as broad statistical proof.

slides.title: Limitations and Future Work
slides.keyMessage: The workflow is reproducible, but external validity, stochastic variance, and incomplete model tracks remain open.

pairs.limitation: One C# API and local SQL Server
pairs.future: Replicate across frameworks, domains, and cloud environments
Estimate output variance across repeated prompts
Add manual penetration and profiling methods
Separate workload composition from time degradation
Run a fresh paired remediation candidate

slides.speakerNotes: The study has important limitations. It evaluates one C# API, one database-backed financial domain, and one local host. Repeated stochastic runs were not performed, so model-output variance is unknown. SonarQube, ZAP, and JMeter each have detection limits and cannot replace manual security review or production observability. The mixed-workload drift rule confounds the final request composition with time-based degradation. Finally, the new-API v2 JMeter comparison is incomplete because a valid GPT-5.4 remediation candidate does not exist. Future work should address each of these limitations directly rather than simply expanding the number of metrics.
slides.transition: Within those boundaries, the final answer to the research problem is clear.
slides.overclaimWarning: State limitations confidently; do not apologize or weaken measured findings.

slides.title: Conclusion
slides.keyMessage: AI-assisted remediation is useful when evidence and human controls decide what ships.

takeaways: Measured gains across quality, security, and latency
Human review and independent tools remained essential
The strongest contribution is the controlled audit-to-fix workflow
visibleContent.closing: Use the model to propose. Use evidence to decide.

slides.speakerNotes: In conclusion, this study shows that ChatGPT or Codex can be useful as a remediation advisor when it operates inside a controlled engineering process. The original study closed retained Sonar findings, cleared gated business-endpoint ZAP alerts, and achieved large p95 latency reductions. The model comparison shows real trade-offs rather than a universal winner. Human review, focused tests, branch isolation, and independent remeasurement are what make the results defensible. The central lesson is simple: use the model to propose, but use evidence to decide. Thank you. I welcome your questions.
slides.transition: Open the appendix only when a question requires detailed evidence.
slides.overclaimWarning: End after the final sentence; do not continue summarizing.

rows: 0% errors; drift gate passed in normalized runs

questions.question: What is the main original contribution of this thesis?
questions.shortAnswer: The contribution is a branch-isolated, scanner-gated workflow that evaluates LLM-assisted remediation across code quality, security, and performance on one production-complexity financial API.
questions.followUpAnswer: The thesis contributes measured before-and-after evidence, preserves finding-to-patch traceability, and shows where conclusions must remain limited. It does not claim a new model or universal ranking.
questions.caution: Do not describe the workflow as fully autonomous.

questions.question: Why is this research important to software engineering?
questions.shortAnswer: It addresses the slow audit-to-fix cycle by testing whether an LLM can help interpret three different tool outputs while evidence and human review control acceptance.
questions.followUpAnswer: Organizations already use static analyzers, security scanners, and load tests. The study connects those findings to a disciplined remediation loop rather than evaluating code generation in isolation.
questions.caution: Do not claim measured developer-productivity improvement.

questions.question: What is the single most important finding?
questions.shortAnswer: The strongest finding is that measurable gains are possible when the model proposes changes but independent tools and human review decide what is accepted.
questions.followUpAnswer: The Sonar closure, ZAP business gate, and p95 reductions support the process, while the drift caveat and model trade-offs show why uncontrolled trust would be inappropriate.
questions.caution: Choose the workflow finding, not one isolated metric.

questions.question: Why did you include the GPT-5.4 versus GPT-5.5 comparison?
questions.shortAnswer: It tests whether a newer model changes remediation quality, patch size, and tool outcomes under comparable evidence workflows.
questions.followUpAnswer: The comparison reveals trade-offs: Sonar is tied, GPT-5.4 has cleaner residual ZAP output, and GPT-5.5 is more balanced in JMeter with smaller patches. That is more informative than declaring a winner.
questions.caution: Do not claim the comparison is exhaustive across prompts or tasks.

questions.question: What would a practitioner do differently after reading this thesis?
questions.shortAnswer: They would place LLM advice behind isolated branches, focused regression tests, and the same scanner or load tool that produced the original finding.
questions.followUpAnswer: They should archive prompts and findings, constrain patch scope, preserve domain invariants, and reject suggestions that do not improve the independent evidence.
questions.caution: Present this as a recommended workflow, not a guaranteed outcome.

questions.question: Why is this thesis-level work rather than a software project report?
questions.shortAnswer: It frames research questions, controls branch-level comparisons, defines acceptance criteria, collects multi-tool evidence, analyzes trade-offs, and states validity limits.
questions.followUpAnswer: The web application is an artifact, but the thesis contribution is the empirical design and interpretation across reproducible measurements, not simply implementation of the API.
questions.caution: Do not center the answer on the user interface.

questions.question: How can you attribute improvements to ChatGPT rather than normal developer work?
questions.shortAnswer: The thesis evaluates an AI-assisted human workflow, not the model alone; prompts, model suggestions, human decisions, branches, tests, and reruns provide process attribution.
questions.followUpAnswer: A human remained necessary, so the causal unit is the combined process. Branch isolation supports before/after attribution, but it does not separate model skill from reviewer skill completely.
questions.caution: Do not claim pure model causality.

questions.question: Why did you use only one codebase?
questions.shortAnswer: The study prioritizes deep, traceable evaluation of one production-complexity financial API; this strengthens internal traceability but limits external validity.
questions.followUpAnswer: Replication across frameworks, languages, domains, and deployment environments is required before generalizing the effect size.
questions.caution: Acknowledge the limitation directly.

questions.question: Why did you not repeat each model run multiple times?
questions.shortAnswer: The study controls one archived run per task through branch and prompt traceability, but it does not estimate stochastic output variance.
questions.followUpAnswer: Repeated identical prompts with confidence intervals over fix acceptance, patch size, and final metrics would be the correct next experiment.
questions.caution: Do not suggest deterministic model behavior.

questions.question: Is a before-and-after branch comparison enough to prove causality?
questions.shortAnswer: No. It supports attribution under controlled environment and branch conditions, but it is not a randomized causal experiment.
questions.followUpAnswer: The design keeps the host, runtime, database, data, and measurement tool stable and isolates fix classes. Remaining confounders include warm-up state, caches, and unobserved branch interactions.
questions.caution: Use 'supports attribution,' not 'proves causation.'

questions.question: How did you prevent cherry-picking successful recommendations?
questions.shortAnswer: The workflow preserves raw findings, scoped prompts, human-effort traceability, regression tests, and rerun evidence, while the report also records remaining risks and incomplete tracks.
questions.followUpAnswer: The study would be stronger with a complete attempt-level acceptance/rejection dataset across repeated runs. The current report improves transparency but does not eliminate selection bias completely.
questions.caution: Do not claim perfect elimination of selection bias.

questions.question: Why are there different baseline finding counts, 28 retained findings and 21 code smells?
questions.shortAnswer: Twenty-eight is the retained C# finding set used for remediation traceability; 21 is the SonarQube code-smell metric. They are related but not identical measures.
questions.followUpAnswer: The report keeps both because the retained finding set includes rule-level evidence used by the workflow, while the dashboard metric categorizes code smells separately.
questions.caution: Never label all 28 as code smells or vulnerabilities.

questions.question: Can you claim the API is secure because ZAP has no High, Medium, or Low business alerts?
questions.shortAnswer: No. I can claim that the pre-registered ZAP business-endpoint gate was met under the tested configuration.
questions.followUpAnswer: ZAP is a dynamic scanner with coverage limits. Manual penetration testing, threat modeling, dependency monitoring, and production controls are still necessary.
questions.caution: Avoid the phrase 'completely secure.'

questions.question: Why did informational alerts remain after remediation?
questions.shortAnswer: Informational alerts are observations rather than gated vulnerabilities, and some reflect authentication fingerprints, local HTTP transport, Swagger, or static assets.
questions.followUpAnswer: The report retains them for transparency. In the model comparison, these residuals are why GPT-5.4 has cleaner ZAP output than GPT-5.5 even though both pass the business-endpoint gate.
questions.caution: Do not hide or dismiss residual alerts.

questions.question: How did you test authorization?
questions.shortAnswer: Authenticated scans and role-based tests covered Admin, FinanceManager, User, and Auditor against protected account, period, journal, report, and audit operations.
questions.followUpAnswer: Unauthorized attempts are expected to return 403, and the application evidence also shows restricted Auditor navigation and read-only access.
questions.caution: Do not claim exhaustive authorization proof for every future route.

questions.question: What security fixes had the largest effect?
questions.shortAnswer: Applying security headers before Swagger/OpenAPI, reducing exposed diagnostic UI, and updating vulnerable dependencies cleared the main gated alert families.
questions.followUpAnswer: The ordering matters because middleware placed after Swagger does not protect those responses. The fix was configuration and dependency focused rather than a claim of redesigning the entire security architecture.
questions.caution: Tie each fix to observed alert families.

questions.question: Did you test SQL injection and CSRF?
questions.shortAnswer: ZAP coverage included injection-related checks, and no gated SQL-injection result remained; CSRF interpretation is limited because the API uses JWT rather than a cookie-based browser session for its core contract.
questions.followUpAnswer: Scanner coverage does not replace manual parameterized-query review. CSRF risk depends on credential transport and browser behavior, so it must be interpreted in the actual authentication design.
questions.caution: Do not claim a manual penetration test was performed.

questions.question: Could caching financial responses expose one user's data to another?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes if cache keys or authorization boundaries are incorrect, so cache scope, account identity, expiry, and invalidation must be reviewed as security constraints.
questions.followUpAnswer: The thesis treats caching as an optimization subject to authorization and accounting invariants. Future production use should add explicit cross-user cache-isolation tests and distributed-cache threat analysis.
questions.caution: Do not claim the local cache design proves multi-tenant isolation.

questions.question: Why focus on p95 and p99 instead of average latency?
questions.shortAnswer: Tail percentiles show the slow experience hidden by averages and are more sensitive to report-query and contention problems.
questions.followUpAnswer: p95 is the threshold below which 95 percent of requests complete; p99 captures rarer but important slow requests. Throughput and error rate are interpreted alongside them.
questions.caution: Do not define p95 as an average.

questions.question: Why did p500 appear faster than p100 in the baseline totals?
questions.shortAnswer: The profiles have different request mixes and timing, so total p95 values are not guaranteed to increase monotonically with the profile label.
questions.followUpAnswer: This is exactly why endpoint-level results and workload composition matter. The comparison is valid within each profile before versus after, not as a simple cross-profile scalability curve.
questions.caution: Do not invent a hardware explanation without telemetry.

questions.question: What caused the largest latency improvements?
questions.shortAnswer: The main changes removed report-snapshot writes from read paths, reused aggregated balances, added indexes, reduced repeated queries, and cached account-ledger output.
questions.followUpAnswer: Trial balance, profit and loss, balance sheet, and account ledger endpoints had the largest visible reductions, especially under spike load.
questions.slideRef: S15 and Table 4.5 in A05 context
questions.caution: Do not attribute every millisecond to one change.

questions.question: Why did the original drift heuristic still fail when latency improved?
questions.shortAnswer: The last measurement window had a heavier request composition, so the aggregate drift metric mixed workload change with time-based degradation.
questions.followUpAnswer: A better design would calculate drift per endpoint or keep request composition constant across windows before aggregating.
questions.caution: Do not describe the drift failure as a hidden system failure or ignore it.

questions.question: Were the load tests run in a production environment?
questions.shortAnswer: No. They were run on one controlled Windows 11 host with a local SQL Server database and fixed JMeter container.
questions.followUpAnswer: That design improves repeatability for branch comparison but limits absolute performance generalization to cloud, distributed, or multi-node production systems.
questions.caution: Do not call local latency a production SLA result.

questions.question: How do you know caching did not make the accounting data stale?
questions.shortAnswer: The acceptance workflow preserves posting, balance, audit, and regression checks, but production cache invalidation deserves deeper dedicated testing.
questions.followUpAnswer: The safe rule is to invalidate or version cache entries on relevant journal and account mutations and to test post-write reads explicitly.
questions.caution: Do not claim exhaustive cache-consistency proof.

questions.question: Would a competent developer have made the same fixes without ChatGPT?
questions.shortAnswer: Possibly. The thesis does not compare developer-only productivity; it evaluates whether the AI-assisted workflow produced acceptable measured outcomes.
questions.followUpAnswer: A controlled human-only comparison with time-on-task and review effort would be needed to claim productivity or superiority over expert remediation.
questions.caution: Do not claim time savings were measured.

questions.question: Are you simply optimizing for the tools rather than improving the software?
questions.shortAnswer: That risk exists, so the workflow combines three independent tools, regression tests, accounting invariants, and visible application behavior.
questions.followUpAnswer: Even this triangulation is incomplete. Manual code review and production observability remain necessary, but cross-tool consistency reduces the chance of optimizing one dashboard only.
questions.caution: Acknowledge Goodhart's-law risk.

questions.question: Why should we trust model identity and provenance?
questions.shortAnswer: Identity follows controller-assigned task provenance, isolated branches or worktrees, commit hashes, archived task logs, and paired measurement records.
questions.followUpAnswer: The fresh v2 measurements scan model-produced source code; the tools do not invoke an LLM during measurement. Historical GPT-5.4 process evidence is less complete and is disclosed as such.
questions.caution: Distinguish controller provenance from independent cryptographic attestation.

questions.question: Why did GPT-5.5 have almost as many authenticated ZAP instances as the baseline?
questions.shortAnswer: Raw instance counts include repeated informational and non-business observations; the gate is interpreted by severity, class, and endpoint, not volume alone.
questions.followUpAnswer: GPT-5.5 cleared the major business security-header problems but retained more Swagger, static-asset, and local-transport residuals, so GPT-5.4 is correctly reported as cleaner on ZAP.
questions.caution: Do not use only the pass label; acknowledge the residual volume.

questions.question: Is the new-API v2 comparison fair if GPT-5.4 lacks a JMeter candidate?
questions.shortAnswer: It is fair only for the paired SonarQube and ZAP tracks; it is not valid for an overall three-tool ranking.
questions.followUpAnswer: The report explicitly marks JMeter not scored and requires a fresh GPT-5.4 remediation run before any three-tool conclusion.
questions.caution: Never treat the challenge baseline as GPT-5.4 remediation output.

questions.question: What result would falsify your main conclusion?
questions.shortAnswer: If repeated controlled runs failed to reproduce tool improvements, introduced domain regressions, or required more review effort than conventional remediation, the practical claim would weaken.
questions.followUpAnswer: The thesis conclusion is conditional: usefulness depends on bounded prompts, human review, independent gates, and repeatable evidence. Removing those conditions changes the claim.
questions.caution: Answer with falsifiable conditions, not defensiveness.

runs.name: Content run
runs.goal: Explain each slide without reading and mark unfamiliar terms.

runs.name: Timing run
runs.goal: Finish the main deck in 27-28 minutes and shorten only notes, not evidence.

runs.name: Defense run
runs.goal: Present once, then answer ten hostile questions using the appendix.

answerMethod: Answer the question in one sentence.
recoveryPhrases: The evidence I can support is...
That is outside the measured scope of this study; the relevant limitation is...
I do not want to overclaim, so I would separate the measured result from the interpretation.
